item.title: Nobody Signed Up to Just Watch It Happen
item.dc:creator: Gagan Jain
item.content:encoded:
I used to write a paragraph, read it back, feel the small friction of a wrong word, and fix it. That friction was the work. Now I type a prompt, watch text assemble itself in seconds, and my job has quietly changed to reading output and deciding if it’s good enough. Same article. Different person doing it. I am no longer the one doing it. I am the one checking.

Nothing about the result is worse. Often it’s faster, cleaner, more consistent than what I would have produced on the fourth draft. But something in me refuses to call this satisfying, and it took a while to understand why.

The task didn’t get easier. It got relocated.

It isn’t just writing. Ask a designer what part of the job they loved. Or a carpenter. Or a photographer. Or a programmer. Very few will say they loved approving the finished product. They loved becoming the reason it existed.

For most of working history, effort and outcome were roped together by time. You wrote the draft, sanded the wood, coded the feature, designed the poster, and the time it took was also the proof that you had done something. Slowness wasn’t a flaw in the system. It was the receipt. The gap between action and consequence was short enough that you could feel your own hand in the result. That feeling has a name, and it isn’t pride exactly. It’s closer to authorship.

Automation doesn’t remove the work. It removes the middle of it. The part where a blank page slowly stops being blank, where a rough shape resolves into a specific one, where you’re wrong three times before you’re right. That middle stretch was never the fun part in the moment, but it was where the sense of having made something came from. Skip it, and what’s left on either side is a request and a verdict. You ask, it answers, you judge. There is no middle to be inside of anymore.

You cannot feel ownership over a stretch of time you were not present for.

This is why the fatigue feels different from old-fashioned busyness. It isn’t the fatigue of too much doing. It’s the fatigue of too much switching, too much checking in on things you didn’t build. Approve this, redirect that, review the draft, redirect again. None of it closes a loop the way finishing something with your own hands used to. You are managing a process instead of having a process. And managing, it turns out, was never the rewarding part. It was always the byproduct.

Notice how little time modern work allows you to stay inside a single thought. Before one task develops enough resistance to become absorbing, another demands your attention. AI didn’t create context switching, but by compressing execution into seconds, it made transitions the dominant unit of work. We no longer spend our day doing tasks. We spend our day transitioning between tasks that are already half-built.

Underneath all of this is something surprisingly basic. We need to be able to point at a piece of the world and say, I caused that. Three hours into solving a stubborn problem, when it finally gives, you can trace the exact moment it happened, and know your own hand was in it. When a tool generates ninety-eight percent of the artifact, that line goes fuzzy. You can no longer trace your way from cause to result. That’s the actual cost. Not the missing hours. The missing chain of cause and effect.

Efficiency was supposed to buy back time. Instead it bought back the part of the task that made the time worth spending.

A content designer who spent a week on a poster wasn’t just producing an asset, they were exercising a kind of taste, testing it against resistance, refining it, watching their own judgment shape the outcome in real time. Now the poster exists in one pass, and that judgment has nowhere left to apply itself except at the very end, as a thumbs up or thumbs down on something someone, or something, else made. Same for the copywriter, the illustrator, the editor. The output improved. The doing evaporated. The trade happened so gradually that most of us noticed the efficiency long before we noticed what had quietly disappeared alongside it.

We used to think automation would free us from work. It may instead be freeing us from the very experiences that made work psychologically rewarding. The problem was never that we’re forbidden from doing the work ourselves. It’s that every incentive increasingly asks why we still would. No one is going to wait a week for a hand-crafted poster when a serviceable one exists in a minute. That much is settled. The stability of “this is simply how the work is done” has already quietly moved, and nobody sent a notice.

Maybe that’s why fulfillment has quietly migrated outside work. It’s probably not a coincidence that so many people are rediscovering the physical world right now. Hiking, sports, long drives with no real destination, trips built around being there rather than optimizing the itinerary. None of it rewards efficiency. A tennis set isn’t better for being quicker. A drive doesn’t improve by shaving off ten minutes. There’s no version of a good hike you can generate in one pass and approve.

The body still has to be present for the outcome to count.

For now. Physical intelligence, the kind that could run the trail, climb the mountain, or swing the racket in your place, hasn’t caught up yet. So these activities have quietly become one of the last stretches of middle that still belongs to whoever is doing it. Not because anyone decided to protect it. Because nothing has been able to take it yet.

Inside work, the same instinct shows up on a smaller scale, and without the luxury of an untouched domain. A hobby kept manual on purpose. One part of the job nobody has automated yet, guarded a little more fiercely than it probably deserves. Not a stand against the market, the market was never going to notice. Just a private, mostly unspoken refusal to let every last stretch of doing be replaced by watching.

Outside those pockets, the feeling returns. Maybe that’s why so many of us finish the day feeling strangely absent from our own accomplishments. The work exists. We just don’t remember being there while it became real.

Perhaps the deepest cost of automation isn’t that machines can now create. It’s that humans are slowly becoming spectators to their own work.

item.title: Your Phone Isn’t the Problem
item.dc:creator: Gagan Jain
item.content:encoded:
I sit down to work and reach for my phone before the first thought fully forms. Not because something urgent has happened, but because nothing has. The absence of stimulation feels like a gap that needs to be filled, and before I have decided anything, my hand has already moved.

A few minutes later, I am technically working. Tabs open, cursor moving, but the attention feels shallow, easily displaced. The task is not difficult. It is simply not holding. It is tempting to blame distraction. Phones, notifications, short-form content. The usual suspects. But the issue begins earlier.

Distraction does not start with the notification. It starts with the desire to leave.

On the tennis court, the experience is different. My mind is not quiet, it is active, almost conversational. Where should the ball go? If I place it wide, what is the likely return? If my opponent moves cross-court, how do I recover? The thoughts arrive quickly, but they do not feel like interruptions. They feel like a single thread unfolding in real time, each one pulling the next into place.

The same happens when I am learning something new. One idea leads to another. A gap in understanding triggers a question, which leads to refinement. And when that chain holds, something quietly changes, ideas stop feeling like separate things and start feeling like a structure you are building. Things stick not because you are trying to remember them, but because each new thought has something to attach to. At some point, time drops out of awareness, not because the experience is mystical, but because nothing has broken the chain.

In both cases, the structure is the same. Attention continues!

We tend to think of flow as something rare or peak-like, a special state reserved for moments of high performance or intensity. But experientially, it feels much simpler than that. Flow is what thinking feels like when it is allowed to continue. Not faster thinking. Not deeper thinking. Just uninterrupted thinking. The mind does not go silent in flow. It becomes single-threaded.

Most of the time, that thread does not survive. A task begins, but before the loop can close, before action leads to feedback and adjustment, the attention shifts. A notification appears. A tab opens. A thought about something else intrudes. The chain resets, and we are back at the beginning.

We do not struggle to focus. We struggle to continue.

Leaving has become nearly frictionless. The cost of exit is close to zero, and what you exit toward is almost always more immediately rewarding than what you left. This is not a character flaw. The brain responds to novelty with a small, reliable signal of interest, a nudge toward the new thing. Unresolved work does not offer that. It offers the mild discomfort of incompleteness, of not yet knowing, of a loop that has not closed. So the pull toward the phone is not weakness. It is a mismatch between what the brain rewards now and what the work will offer later.

The notification does not interrupt. It justifies a departure already in motion.

This is the part that is easy to skip over. Attention does not just drift. It defects. It moves toward what we are willing to engage with, and away from what we are not. And the reason we are unwilling is usually not that the task is too hard. It is that the early stretch of any task has a particular texture to it. Nothing has clicked yet. The shape of the problem is still unclear, and that unclarity has a physical quality, a kind of restlessness, like holding a question you cannot yet form properly. The mind does not sit easily there. It wants resolution, and if the work is not offering it yet, it will look for it elsewhere.

So we leave. And then we come back. And then we leave again. Most of our time is not spent thinking. It is spent restarting thinking.

Flow feels rare because it requires staying through that early stretch, long enough for the loop to close, for one thought to lead to the next, for the work to become coherent enough to hold attention on its own.

That shift does happen. Most people never find out, because they left a few minutes before it did.

item.title: The Broken Feedback Loop of Adulthood
item.dc:creator: Gagan Jain
item.content:encoded:
“Swimming takes only a month to learn, I’ll do it soon.” I said this to myself ten years ago. The month never arrived. Not because I decided against it. There was no decision. No morning where I weighed it and chose otherwise. It simply stayed where I put it, pending, quiet, never urgent enough to move.

Where did the signal go?

For most of childhood, someone was always tracking your progress. A teacher recorded whether you were improving. A coach noticed your form. A parent registered whether you seemed okay. The environment was instrumented. Feedback arrived continuously, even when it was unwelcome.

The cruelty is structural. The more reliably childhood confirmed your behavior, the more completely adulthood’s silence undoes it. Continuous reinforcement produces learning that depends on continued confirmation: when the reward stops, the absence is felt immediately and the behavior collapses. The schedule that made learning easiest is the one that makes unlearning fastest.

Adulthood removes the visible schedule. Not abruptly, but gradually, and without announcement. It does not punish you for the behaviors childhood rewarded. It simply stops confirming them. The friendship you are quietly neglecting will not signal distress until the distance has already become the default. The habit you meant to build remains pending, exactly where you left it, with no record of when it stopped being imminent.

This is not a collection of separate failures. It is one process, unfolding in stages.

In adulthood, the gap between action and consequence grows long enough that the connection weakens enough to stop reliably updating behavior. When outcomes can no longer be attributed to actions, updates degrade. A signal sustained long enough without response stops feeling like noise. It starts feeling like truth, and behavior reorganizes around it.

The system stops updating, not from defeat but from inference: my actions do not determine what happens to me. And by the time that conclusion becomes visible through crisis: the relationship that finally breaks, the body that finally registers the cost, the gap has already compounded beyond the reach of any single adjustment.

The vague, floating dissatisfaction many adults carry often has this cause. It is not laziness. It is not ingratitude. It is the accurate sensation of navigating without instruments that were once provided automatically.

At some point you stopped trying new things and called it knowing yourself. You have a type of person you get along with, refined over years. You stopped meeting people outside it and called it knowing what you value in friendship. The friendships you might have had remain theoretical. They never failed. They were never pursued.

The policy that got you here becomes the only policy you run: high confidence, low variance, endlessly repeated. Not because it is best, but because nothing contradicts it strongly enough to displace it. The better alternative doesn’t disappear. It is never tried. And every repetition increases the distance from it. The distance never feels like a decision.

The steps you’ve been taking all these years never get the small corrections that would have changed them.

The scaffolding came down. Nobody said anything. Nothing replaced it.

item.title: Why Does Stability Feel Like Background Noise?
item.dc:creator: Gagan Jain
item.content:encoded:
On paper, my job is the stable one. It pays my rent, compounds over time, and offers a clear trajectory. It is the rational choice. And yet the hours I spend on the tennis court, exhausting and ego-bruising and guaranteeing nothing, are the ones I anticipate. The contrast is difficult to ignore.

Why does the thing that funds my life feel ambient, while the thing with no safety net feels vivid and central?

It is tempting to blame feedback loops. Tennis offers immediate causality. I swing, I see the result, I adjust. Work unfolds differently. Effort stretches across months, filtered through meetings, coordination, and review cycles. The sentence I write today does not visibly connect to the chapter that closes half a year from now. The arc is long and the connection between action and outcome is mediated.

But the deeper difference is not about timing. It is about authorship.

On the court, causality is direct. If I improve, the scoreboard reflects it. If I falter, it is traceable to my own decisions. The loop between action and consequence is tight, and because it is tight, I feel unmistakably like the protagonist.

In stable work, causality is negotiated. My effort moves through systems of alignment, incentives, dependencies, and collaboration. Outcomes are collective and distributed. Wins are rarely attributable to a single swing; losses are rarely catastrophic for a single mistake. This dilution of agency is not an accident. It is the mechanism by which stability is produced.

Stability is a silent contract. In exchange for lower variance and predictable compounding, I surrender some degree of authorship. I trade the volatility of being a decisive actor for the reliability of being a component in a larger machine. The system works precisely because no single person’s swing determines the score.

That trade has psychological consequences. Humans remember chapters, not days. We recall the exam that compressed a year of preparation into three charged hours. We remember the message we waited for because it condensed uncertainty and desire into a single moment. Those experiences concentrate agency and stakes.

Most workdays, by contrast, are part of an ongoing manual written collectively. The plot advances, but rarely because of a single decisive act. Variance is dampened. Outcomes are smoothed. The drama is intentionally reduced.

If work feels like background noise, it may not be because it lacks importance. It may be because it is performing its function well. It reduces volatility. It absorbs shocks. It ensures continuity. The absence of drama is evidence of structural soundness.

Tennis feels like a main plot because every swing matters. Work feels ambient because no single swing is allowed to.

The question, then, is not how to make stability thrilling. It is whether I am comfortable with the exchange it demands.

High agency and high variance come together. So do stability and negotiated causality. If I want the protections of one, I cannot be surprised by the texture of the other.

Stability does not feel like background noise by mistake. It feels that way because smoothing the noise is exactly what it was designed to do.
